title: The lump of salt
hookLine: Yajnavalkya drops salt in water, says there's no awareness after death, and Maitreyi says: now you've confused me
carry: the salt isn't gone; it's everywhere
tomorrow: the honey doctrine — all beings are honey for each other
last: HEAR IT, REFLECT ON IT, DWELL IN IT.

cards: A lump of salt, dropped into water overnight. In the morning it's gone, yet every sip is salty, here, and here. Twenty days ago, in the Chandogya, a father used that salt to teach his son.
Today, in a different book, a different teacher picks it up: Yajnavalkya, still talking with Maitreyi. And this time the salt says something she can't follow. She tells him so, out loud.

teach.h: SALT DISSOLVES; THE WATER IS SALTY.
teach.b: As a lump of salt thrown into water dissolves, he says, and you can't pick it out again, but wherever you take the water from it's salty, so this great being, endless, without limit, is nothing but a mass of knowing.
It rises up out of these elements, and vanishes back into them.
Then the hard line: after death, there is no awareness. Maitreyi stops him. That's where you've confused me.
It sounds as if the deathless self she asked for just dissolved into nothing. Yajnavalkya says: I'm saying nothing confusing. Listen.
Where there seems to be two, one sees another, hears another, knows another. But where everything has become one's own self, then by what, and whom, would one see?

teach.h: BY WHAT WOULD ONE KNOW THE KNOWER?
teach.b: By what would one know the knower? So the salt isn't gone. It's everywhere.
What ends is the gap between a knower and something known.
When the scene is told again later in the book, the salt image grows sharper, and gives today its title: a lump of salt has no inside and no outside; it's taste all the way through.

So this self has no inside, no outside; it's knowing all the way through. Schools of Vedanta read the dissolving differently. For Advaita, the separate knower melts like the salt, and only pure consciousness is left.
Other schools read that line, no awareness after death, as the end of the narrow, body-bound kind of knowing, not of the soul itself. Neither reading turns the self into nothing.
That's the Hindu teaching on death under this story: the atman isn't destroyed.

teach.h: NOT BORN, AND DOES NOT DIE.
teach.b: At a death, Hindus often turn to the Bhagavad Gita's words: the self is not born, and it does not die.

teach.h: THE SALT ISN'T GONE; IT'S EVERYWHERE.
teach.b: Maitreyi's confusion is the right question, asked out loud.

how: Teachers of Vedanta use the salt image, from both the Chandogya and the Brihadaranyaka, to explain how the self pervades everything; this passage is read and debated in Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita commentaries alike.

o: a mass of knowing, all the way through
a solid lump of salt left in water
a deep trance where knowing stops

games.q: what's inside the passage — tap the pairs.
p: dissolves; the water is salty everywhere

s: the salt-in-water image appears in only one Upanishad
Uddalaka uses it in the Chandogya; Yajnavalkya uses it here, for a different point.
Maitreyi tells Yajnavalkya he has confused her
after he says there's no awareness after death.
Yajnavalkya means the self becomes nothing
what ends is the gap between knower and known; the salt is everywhere.

games.q: you're Maitreyi. your husband says that after death there is no awareness. what do you do?
o: tell him plainly: here, you've confused me.
decide he doesn't know after all.
games.why: she says it out loud, and he explains: where all has become the self, by what would one see whom? by what would one know the knower?

practice: Close your eyes and listen to the sounds around you: a car, a fan, your own breath. Notice that you can't find the edge where a sound stops being out there and starts being heard in here; it's hearing, all the way through.
When a thought builds the wall again, me in here, the world out there, let it dissolve like the salt.

wordCard.voice: Vijnanaghana, a mass of knowing. Gone from sight, yet taste all the way through: the self, knowing all the way through, like a dissolved lump of salt.

orig.note: Sanskrit vijñāna (knowing) + ghana (solid, dense): a mass of knowing, like a lump of salt.

carryVoice: Your line: the salt isn't gone; it's everywhere. Tomorrow, the honey teaching, and a sage with a horse's head. That's day three hundred sixty-nine.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.20 (the self is not born and does not die)
